findings.paper_title: NMD Trading Account 2025-26 Outturn Q4
findings.headline: Building Control partnership delivers £128,441 deficit, outperforming budget by £99,579
findings.detail: The NDC-MDDC Building Control partnership incurred expenditure of £814,404 against income of £685,963. While this creates a deficit requiring general fund subsidy, actual spending came in significantly below the budgeted deficit of £228,020, demonstrating effective cost control across both councils.
findings.matters: The service requires recurring general fund support to cover the income gap, which impacts the councils' financial sustainability. The substantial favorable variance signals strong financial management and realistic cost discipline in a partnership arrangement.
findings.figures: Actual deficit £128,441 (NDC £84,834, MDDC £43,607); budgeted deficit £228,020; variance £99,579
findings.quote: Total Actual Variance To Budget Spend -99,579

findings.paper_title: Annual Treasury Management Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Market expectations point to higher inflation and sustained or rising interest rates through 2027 due to Middle East conflict
findings.detail: The treasury report notes that as of early April 2026, market sentiment is dominated by Middle East conflict concerns, with commentators anticipating rising inflation risk. Rates are not expected to be cut for some time, and may need to increase to counteract inflationary pressures from energy costs through 2027.
findings.matters: Rising borrowing rates will increase debt service costs on the council's £36.3m capital financing requirement and any future capital borrowing
findings.figures: PWLB rates at 31 March 2026: 1-year 5.04%, 5-year 5.28%, 10-year 5.72%, 25-year 6.29%
findings.quote: More recently, the Middle East conflict is likely to see inflation spike higher from late spring 2026 through to early 2027

findings.paper_title: Annual Treasury Management Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Interest costs saved £277k due to capital slippages and internal borrowing strategy
findings.detail: Interest paid on borrowing was £542,626 at 4.16% average rate, against a budget assumption of £820,000, a 34% underspend. The council attributes this saving to slippages in the capital spending and its choice to rely on internal borrowing and delayed external borrowing.
findings.matters: While this year benefited from delayed costs, the strategy of internal borrowing means future external borrowing will be required to replenish reserves
findings.figures: Interest paid £542,626 at 4.16% average rate vs budget £820,000
findings.quote: £542,626 interest was paid at an average rate of 4.16% on the loans during the financial year. This compares to a budget assumption of £820,000 in interest cost. Slippages in the capital spend, our strategy of internal borrowing and delaying the external borrowing allowed us to reduce the borrowing costs in year.

findings.paper_title: Annual Treasury Management Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Council maintained under-borrowed position with £13.55m of internal borrowing against £30.55m capital financing requirement
findings.detail: The council did not fully fund its Capital Financing Requirement through external borrowing, instead using cash from reserves and working capital balances for £13.55m of the £30.55m CFR. External borrowing was only £17m, representing significant reliance on reserves to cover the gap.
findings.matters: Using reserves for borrowing depletes the council's liquidity cushion for contingencies and suggests limited additional external borrowing capacity
findings.figures: CFR £30.55m; external borrowing £17m; internal borrowing £13.55m
findings.quote: During 2025/26, the Authority maintained an under-borrowed position. This meant that the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement), was not fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Authority's reserves, balances and cash flow was used as an interim measure.

findings.paper_title: Annual Treasury Management Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Capital programme delivered £6.1m below estimate due to slippages including Ilfracombe Healthy Homes project
findings.detail: Actual capital expenditure was £10.917m against an estimate of £17.029m, a 36% shortfall. The council explicitly cited slippages in the capital programme, naming the Ilfracombe Healthy Homes project as an example. Unfinanced capital expenditure came in at £3.537m versus the estimated £6.860m.
findings.matters: Capital programme slippages indicate execution risk and delay the council's strategic investments, raising questions about project delivery capability
findings.figures: Actual £10.917m vs estimate £17.029m; unfinanced capital £3.537m vs estimate £6.860m
findings.quote: The 2025/26 capital programme added additional unfinanced capital expenditure of £3.5m in relation to the Future High Street Project and improvement works to Green Lanes. This was lower than the mid-year estimate due to slippages in the capital programme, including schemes such as the Ilfracombe Healthy Homes project.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Risk management framework not yet adequate for new social housing provider role
findings.detail: The council has identified that its Risk Management Framework and Service Risk Registers need updating to capture risks from becoming a Local Authority Registered Provider. Review is scheduled for September 2026, suggesting governance structures are incomplete for the new venture.
findings.matters: Inadequate risk management for a major new financial undertaking exposes the council to unidentified risks and suggests incomplete preparation
findings.figures: Review due September 2026
findings.quote: To review the Risk Management Framework and Service Risk Registers to ensure that it adequately captures all risks relating to the Council become a Local Authority Registered Provider – September 2026

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Internal audit recommends improving clarity and accessibility of financial reports to support member scrutiny
findings.detail: The council has been advised to improve financial reporting to support member engagement and scrutiny of financial decisions. Reports should be more service-focused with greater narrative context. Deadline for action is December 2026.
findings.matters: Weak financial reporting transparency could mask deteriorating finances or prevent proper oversight of budgets and spending patterns
findings.figures: Action due December 2026
findings.quote: To improve the clarity and accessibility of financial reports to support member engagement and scrutiny of financial decisions. Reports to be more service focused with greater narrative and context to aid understanding

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Council entering direct social housing provision as Local Authority Registered Provider for the first time in over 20 years
findings.detail: The council will directly provide and own social housing units, managed by North Devon Homes under a management agreement. The council engaged external consultants to ensure governance and legal compliance from day one. This represents a significant new financial undertaking with capital and borrowing implications.
findings.matters: New housing ventures of this scale carry financial, borrowing, and operational risks that materially affect council balance sheets and debt capacity
findings.figures: Over 20 years since last direct provision
findings.quote: Looking forward to next year, we be making our first direct provision of social housing, as a Local Authority Registered Provider, for over 20 years

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Council identified a budget gap in Medium Term Financial Strategy requiring active remediation
findings.detail: A Councillor Budget Working Group has been established to proactively review options for closing a gap in the MTFS. The gap was not quantified in this statement, but its existence suggests the council faces a structural funding challenge requiring council-level attention.
findings.matters: Budget gaps and how councils address them through savings, growth, or borrowing are central to lender credit assessment
findings.figures: Gap amount not disclosed
findings.quote: Councillor Budget Working Group to proactively review options for addressing the budget gap in Medium Term Financial Strategy

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Crematorium Joint Committee governance arrangements received limited assurance from internal audit
findings.detail: Internal audit found limited evidence that the crematorium joint agreement has been properly reviewed since 1974. A formal review of governance arrangements with Torridge District Council is required by March 2026, suggesting the council has identified governance gaps over a significant shared asset.
findings.matters: Governance weaknesses in joint ventures are material to lenders assessing the council's control environment and operational risk
findings.figures: Joint agreement sealed in 1974
findings.quote: The Internal Audit review of the Joint Agreement Arrangements for the North Devon Crematorium Joint Committee gave limited assurance. With limited evidence that the arrangements had been reviewed since it was sealed in 1974.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 Lynmouth Harbour PMSC Audit action tracker
findings.headline: Five Port Safety Management Code non-compliance findings remained in-progress beyond their April 2026 remediation deadline
findings.detail: A January 2026 PMSC audit identified five non-compliance findings covering health & safety risk assessments, marine safety planning, and conservancy duties. As of the May 12 board meeting, all five remained marked 'Red' status and 'In Progress' with the target completion date of 29 April 2026 passed. This represents a missed regulatory remediation deadline.
findings.matters: Unresolved regulatory non-compliance in a council-operated service indicates governance control gaps and creates exposure to enforcement action and potential liability
findings.figures: 5 non-compliance findings, target date 29/04/2026, board meeting date 12/05/2026
findings.quote: No formal occupational H&S task-based risk assessments.Breach of H&S at Work Act

findings.paper_title: Copy of Committee appendix - final outturn
findings.headline: Lynton & Lynmouth Harbour returned a net deficit of £70,478, the second material loss-making harbor operation.
findings.detail: Operating income of £4,446 was far exceeded by operating expenditure of £29,667 and overheads of £45,257, generating a net deficit of £70,478. Combined with the main harbor, the three operations returned approximately £270,000 in deficits.
findings.matters: Multiple significant loss-making operations indicate harbor services as a whole are not self-sustaining and require ongoing council subsidy.
findings.figures: Operating Income £4,446, Operating Expenditure & Maintenance £29,667, Overheads £45,257, Net Deficit £70,478

findings.paper_title: Copy of Committee appendix - final outturn
findings.headline: Main harbor quarterly deficits more than doubled from Q3 (£62,068) to Q4 (£113,124), indicating worsening performance through the year.
findings.detail: Operating deficits started at £15,075 in Q1 and accelerated through the year, particularly in the second half. Q4 deficit of £113,124 more than doubled the Q3 deficit. This progression suggests operational performance deteriorated significantly.
findings.matters: Growing and accelerating deficits through the year signal worsening operational performance and increasing strain on council finances.

findings.paper_title: Copy of Committee appendix - final outturn
findings.headline: Main harbor operation returned a net deficit of £198,961 to the council in 2025-26.
findings.detail: Operating expenditure and maintenance of £786,408 exceeded operating income of £619,547. With overheads of £32,100, the service returned a net deficit of £198,961 to the council. This is a material operational subsidy from the general fund.
findings.matters: A lender must understand whether the council is operating loss-making services and whether these represent a structural drain on finances.
findings.figures: Operating Income £619,547, Operating Expenditure & Maintenance £786,408, Overheads £32,100, Net Deficit £198,961
findings.quote: The expenditure budget excluding capital finance for the 2025-26 financial year is £697,000. The income budget for the 2025-26 financial year is £503,370 returning a net deficit of £193,630 to NDC.

findings.paper_title: Copy of Supplementary - WSC Sea School - final outturn
findings.headline: Ilfracombe Sea School overspent substantially against budget, with net costs of £2,704 against a £500 budget.
findings.detail: The Sea School's final net expenditure was £2,704 compared to a budget of £500, a £2,204 overspend. Supplies & Services costs drove this variance, reaching £34,799 against a budgeted £18,500 (£16,299 over). Income exceeded budget by £14,096, but was insufficient to offset the cost overrun.
findings.matters: A 440% variance on a budgeted service indicates either weak budget forecasting or cost control issues, though the absolute amount is small.
findings.figures: Budget £500, Outturn £2,704, Variance £2,204. Supplies & Services: Budget £18,500, Actual £34,799.
findings.quote: Net expenditure 500 1,650 2,704 2,204

findings.paper_title: Copy of Full Year - Harbour Outturn 2526 v 2425
findings.headline: Ilfracombe Harbour's operating deficit of £198,961 requires ongoing subsidy despite slight year-on-year improvement
findings.detail: Operating income of £619,547 was insufficient to cover operating expenditure and maintenance of £786,408 plus overheads of £32,100. The deficit improved from £205,204 in 2024/25 but remains substantial, indicating the harbour service does not break even.
findings.matters: A revenue-negative service requires ongoing funding from reserves or general fund, raising questions about sustainability and whether the council's reserves can absorb both this and unexpected costs like the Lynton & Lynmouth spike
findings.figures: Operating deficit £198,961 (2025/26) vs £205,204 (2024/25); income £619,547; expenditure and maintenance £786,408
findings.quote: Operating Deficit / (Surplus) 198,961 205,204

findings.paper_title: Copy of Full Year - Harbour Outturn 2526 v 2425
findings.headline: Lynton & Lynmouth Harbour maintenance costs jumped 608% year-on-year, driving operating deficit from £42,976 to £70,478
findings.detail: Operating expenditure and maintenance increased from £4,187 in 2024/25 to £29,667 in 2025/26. This £25,480 increase drove the operating deficit up by £27,502 (64% increase). The document provides no explanation for the sharp maintenance cost increase.
findings.matters: An unexplained £25,480 maintenance cost spike raises questions about whether this is one-off deferred work or represents an elevated ongoing baseline, either of which materially affects reserve sustainability and future budget forecasting
findings.figures: Maintenance £4,187 (2024/25) to £29,667 (2025/26); operating deficit increased from £42,976 to £70,478
findings.quote: Operating Expenditure and Maintenance 29,667 4,187

findings.paper_title: Quarterly Designated Person Port Marine Safety Code Audit Report – Ilfracombe & Lynmouth Harbours
findings.headline: Lynmouth Harbour had no formal Marine Safety Plan at audit and lacks occupational health and safety risk assessments
findings.detail: At the time of the audit, Lynmouth Harbour had not published a formal Marine Safety Plan (a draft was under review). Additionally, an external audit revealed a lack of formal occupational health and safety risk assessments for Council tasks performed at the harbour, though the Town Clerk confirmed these have now been established.
findings.matters: Multiple concurrent compliance gaps, particularly around health and safety risk management, suggest operational control weaknesses
findings.figures: no formal Marine Safety Plan at time of audit; occupational health and safety risk assessments were missing before remediation
findings.quote: An external audit revealed a lack of formal occupational health and safety risk assessments for Council tasks performed at the harbour. The Town Clerk has responded to this issue, confirming that risk assessments have now been established

findings.paper_title: Quarterly Designated Person Port Marine Safety Code Audit Report – Ilfracombe & Lynmouth Harbours
findings.headline: Lynmouth Harbour has a non-compliance on passage plan that was identified in a previous audit and remains unresolved
findings.detail: A non-compliance was recorded because no passage plan is published for Lynmouth Harbour. This issue has been identified in a previous audit, and while the Harbour User group is developing a user guide, an update on progress was still being requested. The persistence of this finding across audits suggests slow remediation.
findings.matters: Unresolved audit findings, especially those persisting from previous audits, indicate governance or follow-up weaknesses that could extend to financial controls
findings.figures: identified in a previous audit; still outstanding as of Q1 2026/27 audit
findings.quote: A non-compliance was recorded as there is no available passage plan published for Lynmouth Harbour. This has been identified in a previous audit

findings.paper_title: Appendix E Revenue Budget 2026-27, Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026 to 2031
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation capital budget doubles in 2026-27 to £2m, signalling rapid escalation in housing/homelessness demand
findings.detail: Capital allocation for temporary accommodation rises from £1m in 2025-26 to £2m in 2026-27, then £1.86m in 2027-28. Total of £4.86m across three years makes this the single largest commitment within Planning, Housing and Health capital spending. The year-on-year doubling in 2026-27 represents significant acceleration of investment in this service.
findings.matters: Escalating capital spend on temporary accommodation indicates the council faces substantial and growing housing/homelessness pressures that cannot be resolved through existing capacity; this signals ongoing revenue cost exposure and service demand that threatens financial resilience
findings.quote: Provision of temporary accommodation 1,000,000 2,000,000 1,856,663 4,856,663

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026/27
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation moratorium could disrupt 2026/27 capital spending and borrowing plans
findings.detail: Council explicitly flags that a moratorium could be introduced during 2026/27 due to Local Government Reorganisation ahead of the new unitary authority vesting on 1 April 2028. Such a moratorium would restrict large capital spends and any unplanned borrowing, creating institutional uncertainty for approved capital schemes.
findings.matters: Moratorium restrictions would disrupt approved capital programme and require emergency replanning; creates policy uncertainty and potential delivery delays for planned services
findings.figures: Potential moratorium timing: 2026/27; LG Reorganisation vesting date: 1 April 2028
findings.quote: Members should note that a moratorium could be introduced during the 2026/27 financial year in relation to Local Government Reorganisation. This might place restrictions in relation to large capital spends or potential capital receipts, ahead of the new unitary authority's vesting date, scheduled for 1 April 2028.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026/27
findings.headline: Mid-year capital programme increase of £4m for temporary accommodation suggests emerging housing demand pressure
findings.detail: In July 2025, Council approved a £4m addition to the capital programme for temporary accommodation purchases, increasing the total authorised borrowing limit to £46.5m. This mid-year addition to planned spending occurred after the original budget was set, suggesting either planned expansion or response to emerging housing demand.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation spending typically reflects homelessness or housing demand increases; mid-year capital additions signal emerging service pressures that may require ongoing funding
findings.figures: Capital programme increase: £4m; new total authorised borrowing limit: £46.5m
findings.quote: Full Council on 16th July 2025, approved for the total authorised borrowing limit to be increase to £46.5m as part of the decision to vary the capital programme by £4m for the purchase of additional temporary accommodation.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026/27
findings.headline: Council betting on interest rate falls while maintaining short-term borrowing structure creates refinancing risk
findings.detail: North Devon is deliberately under-borrowed (external debt £14m vs CFR £38.9m at end 2025) and plans to keep borrowing short-term to benefit from forecast rate falls. Treasury advisors forecast 5-year PWLB rates falling from 4.81% to 4.10% by end 2027. However, if rates rise sharply instead of falling, the council will face refinancing short-term debt at higher cost, pressuring revenue budgets.
findings.matters: Interest rate forecasts carry significant uncertainty; a sharp rate rise would increase debt servicing costs and reduce funds available for core services
findings.figures: External debt 31/12/25: £14m; CFR 2025/26 estimate: £38.910m; Current 5-year PWLB rate 4.81%, forecast target 4.10%
findings.quote: Given the interest rate forecasts, borrowing will be kept short term so that the Council can benefit from lower borrowing rates on maturity.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026/27
findings.headline: Fund balances declining 51% by 2028/29, reducing financial resilience and increasing borrowing dependence
findings.detail: General Fund reserves are declining from £11.075m (2024/25) to £5.450m (2028/29), a 51% reduction. Total cash available to invest declines from £18.175m to £10.050m over the same period. This represents a significant drawdown of the council's financial buffer and increases dependence on external borrowing to manage cash flow and finance capital.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce a council's financial resilience and ability to absorb cash flow timing issues, service cost shocks, or fund emergencies without additional borrowing
findings.figures: Fund balances 2024/25 £11.075m, 2028/29 £5.450m (51% decline); Total cash to invest 2024/25 £18.175m, 2028/29 £10.050m (45% decline)
findings.quote: Fund balances / reserves 11,075 7,438 7,138 6,000 5,450

findings.paper_title: Appendix C Revenue Budget 2026-27, Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026 to 2031
findings.headline: Total earmarked reserves declined by £125,340 to £5.34m despite £848k in new transfers
findings.detail: Earmarked reserves fell from £5,462,154 at 31 March 2026 to £5,336,814 at 31 March 2027. Despite receiving £848,220 in new transfers into reserves, total outflows of £973,560 (£547k to capital and £426k to revenue) exceeded inflows.
findings.matters: Declining reserves indicate the council is consuming its financial buffers; combined with revenue transfers, this signals tightening financial position and reduced headroom for managing service demand or cost pressures
findings.figures: Opening: £5,462,154; Closing: £5,336,814; Transfers in: £848,220; Transfers out: £973,560

findings.paper_title: Appendix C Revenue Budget 2026-27, Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026 to 2031
findings.headline: Repairs Fund depleted by £296,850, closing at only £219,345
findings.detail: The Repairs Fund opened at £516,195, received £377,860 in new transfers, but had £432,000 transferred to capital and £242,710 to revenue, closing at £219,345. This represents a net reduction of 57% from opening balance.
findings.matters: Drawing down the maintenance reserve to fund both capital work and revenue suggests constrained capacity for future building upkeep and infrastructure maintenance without additional borrowing
findings.figures: Opening: £516,195; Closing: £219,345; Transfers to capital: £432,000; Transfers to revenue: £242,710

findings.paper_title: Appendix C Revenue Budget 2026-27, Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026 to 2031
findings.headline: Council transferred £426,560 from reserves to cover revenue budget in 2026-27
findings.detail: The reserves table shows a transfer from reserves to revenue of £426,560 for the year to 31 March 2027. This indicates the council is using one-off reserve balances to fund ongoing operational costs rather than balancing revenue entirely from current income sources.
findings.matters: Using reserves to cover revenue shortfalls signals structural budget pressures and reduces the council's financial flexibility to absorb future shocks or unexpected costs
findings.figures: £426,560 transferred from reserves to revenue
findings.quote: Transfer from Reserves (to Revenue) -426,560

findings.paper_title: 10 Year Capital Strategy 2026 to 2036
findings.headline: Internal borrowing (reserves deployed to defer external borrowing) will remain tight at £6–£9m, with limited buffer for emergencies or rate-sensitive shortfalls
findings.detail: The Council is maintaining an 'under-borrowed position,' using its own cash (reserves and balances) rather than fully borrowing to fund the CFR. Internal borrowing is projected to remain 'circa £6m' long term and '£8m or above' over the medium term. The strategy notes this 'will need to be reviewed in line with investment returns and counterparty risks,' indicating awareness that low investment yields may not justify holding reserves rather than reducing external debt.
findings.matters: Low internal borrowing reserves mean little buffer against unexpected costs (infrastructure failure, service demand shock) or external funding shocks (reduced government grant); any downturn forces immediate external borrowing or service cuts.
findings.figures: Internal borrowing: ~£6m long term (2030/36), £8m+ medium term (2026/30); total CFR £39m–£44m implies tight cash position
findings.quote: The strategy is also prudently maintaining an under-borrowed position, meaning that as a temporary measure the Council is using its own cash supporting reserves, balances and cash-flows rather than fully funding the CFR with external borrowing. This position will need to be reviewed in line with investment returns and counterparty risks

findings.paper_title: 10 Year Capital Strategy 2026 to 2036
findings.headline: PWLB restrictions on commercial borrowing eliminate yield-based property investment as a revenue offset
findings.detail: Recent changes to Public Works Loan Board lending terms prohibit loans to councils planning to buy commercial assets primarily for yield. As a result, the strategy states: 'no commercial investments will be made.' This removes an option the Council might have used to offset debt service costs through rental or management income.
findings.matters: The loss of PWLB-funded commercial property acquisition reduces the Council's ability to generate offsetting revenue; debt must be serviced from rates, grants, and existing income streams.
findings.figures: No quantified impact; external borrowing remains at £27.5m–£29m regardless
findings.quote: recent changes to the PWLB lending terms mean that they will no longer lend to local authorities that have plans to buy commercial assets primarily for yield within their capital programme. Given the level the external borrowing required over the ten year period and that PWLB would currently be the best option for the Council to borrow these funds, no commercial investments will be made

findings.paper_title: 10 Year Capital Strategy 2026 to 2036
findings.headline: Future capital investment is frozen unless externally funded or revenue-neutral; commercialisation is essential but not detailed
findings.detail: Section 4.7 states: 'Future capital projects would have to have no or limited impact on the revenue budget gap. Any additional borrowing costs would have to be offset by additional income such as a management fee, rental income or additional capital receipts would need to be identified.' Section 4.9 calls the 'long-term outlook...strongly supports the need for the Council to become more efficient and commercially minded...to generate additional income.' However, no specific income targets or commercialisation roadmap are provided.
findings.matters: The capital programme is essentially exhausted; future investment (vehicle electrification, asset maintenance, housing, regeneration) requires commercial or government funding that is not yet secured.
findings.figures: No quantified commercialisation income targets; business-as-usual capital spend £1.3m–£3.5m annually on vehicles, ICT, maintenance, engineering
findings.quote: Future capital projects would have to have no or limited impact on the revenue budget gap. Any additional borrowing costs would have to be offset by additional income

findings.paper_title: 10 Year Capital Strategy 2026 to 2036
findings.headline: Business rates growth reset to zero; the Council has lost all growth achieved since 2013
findings.detail: The government's multi-year funding settlement has reset business rates growth. The 2026/27 budget 'includes no further business rates growth.' Future growth from 2027/28 onward 'has not been factored into the projections yet,' meaning the base case assumes no recovery. This represents a permanent loss of anticipated income.
findings.matters: Loss of business rates growth removes a traditional source of additional revenue; the council must fund the £1.8–£3.1m deficits from cuts or commercialisation alone.
findings.figures: No business rates growth factored into 2026/27–2029/30 forecasts; cumulative loss since 2013 reset is material but unquantified
findings.quote: The financial settlement has reset business rates growth achieved since 2013 and therefore the 2026/27 budget includes no further business rates growth

findings.paper_title: 10 Year Capital Strategy 2026 to 2036
findings.headline: Annual debt service costs rising from £2.3m to £3.6m by 2028/29, then staying above £3.5m long term, adding direct pressure to revenue budget
findings.detail: The total annual cost of capital borrowing (MRP and interest on external borrowing plus finance leases) is projected to reach £3.6m in 2028/29 and remain above £3.5m thereafter. The strategy explicitly warns: 'the annual borrowing cost will keep adding pressure on the Council's revenue budget each year.' This cost is already baked into the forecast deficits.
findings.matters: Debt service crowds out discretionary spending; if revenue deficits persist, the Council will be forced to cut services to meet debt obligations.
findings.quote: The projected cost of borrowing, both external borrowing and long term liabilities, is set to remain above £3.5m per annum over the 6 year forecast period

findings.paper_title: 10 Year Capital Strategy 2026 to 2036
findings.headline: External borrowing to surge from £14m to £29m—a 107% increase—within three years
findings.detail: The Council's external debt is projected to more than double over the medium term: from £14m currently to £20m by March 2026, then to £29m by 2027/28. This peak borrowing is driven by capital schemes already committed (Leisure Centre, Green Lanes Shopping Centre, Future High Streets, temporary accommodation property purchases). After 2028, it reduces only marginally to £27.5m long term.
findings.matters: This scale and speed of borrowing increase signals rising debt service pressure and reduced financial flexibility; any external funding shortfall or interest rate movement will force service cuts.
findings.quote: Total external borrowing as at March 2026 is projected to be £20m (currently external borrowing is £14m), increasing by £9m over the medium term to peak at £29m during 2027/28

findings.paper_title: 10 Year Capital Strategy 2026 to 2036
findings.headline: Revenue budget gap of £1.8m in 2027/28 growing to £3.1m by 2035/36, with no funding plan in place
findings.detail: The Council projects deficits from 2027/28 onward: £1.8m in 2027/28, £2.4m in 2028/29, rising to £3.1m by 2034/35. These forecasts assume only the cost of capital borrowing—no new savings or income measures—and remain unresolved in the strategy. The document explicitly states members 'will be faced with challenging decisions to make as part of setting future budgets.'
findings.matters: A structural deficit of this scale indicates the council cannot sustain services at current levels and will require material cuts, asset sales, or income generation to balance.
findings.quote: for 2027/28 current projections show a medium term financial strategy budget gap of £1.8m increasing to £2.6m by 2029/30

findings.paper_title: Appendix D Revenue Budget 2026-27, Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026 to 2031
findings.headline: Uncertain income assumptions on Extended Producer Responsibility grant and renewable energy income
findings.detail: Two material income streams carry forecast risk. The EPR grant (£1.690m for 2026-27) carries explicit uncertainty: 'stated that payments in future years may change as a result of data collection and modelling.' Renewable energy from business rates is built in at £750k prudently but latest estimates are £840k—suggesting the document may be understating income or using outdated figures.
findings.matters: Income volatility creates forecast risk. If grants are lower than assumed or business rates income disappoints, actual deficits will exceed the paper's forecasts, requiring faster reserve draws or unplanned savings.
findings.figures: EPR grant 2026-27 £1.690m; renewable energy income built in at £750k (latest estimate £840k)
findings.quote: stated that payments in future years may change as a result of data collection and modelling

findings.paper_title: Appendix D Revenue Budget 2026-27, Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026 to 2031
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation proceeding with no additional government funding for transition costs
findings.detail: The council is preparing for a new Unitary authority by 2028 but faces a funding gap for transition. The document states: 'government have confirmed that there is no additional funding to cover transition costs to implement LGR.' North Devon is setting aside £175k per year for initial costs but notes this may not be sufficient.
findings.matters: Reorganisation is a material operational and financial event. Unfunded transition costs will consume reserves or require savings that conflict with service delivery. If LGR does not proceed on schedule, budget assumptions for 2027-28 onwards become invalid.
findings.figures: £175k per year contribution to LGR reserve for 2026-27 and 2027-28. Document assumes only two-year period until new authority forms.
findings.quote: government have confirmed that there is no additional funding to cover transition costs to implement LGR

findings.paper_title: Appendix D Revenue Budget 2026-27, Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026 to 2031
findings.headline: Government funding cut of £876k in 2027-28 (Revenue Support Grant from £5.476m to £4.600m) drives structural gap
findings.detail: Revenue Support Grant falls sharply from £5.476m in 2026-27 to £4.600m in 2027-28—a £876k reduction. It then steps down further to £3.685m for 2028-29 onwards. This government funding reduction is the primary driver of the emerging structural deficit and gives no time to adjust savings.
findings.matters: The largest source of council funding is being cut in the year when deficits emerge. This removes flexibility to adjust and explains why the council cannot grow its way out of the problem.
findings.figures: Revenue Support Grant: 2026-27 £5,476k → 2027-28 £4,600k (£876k reduction) → 2028-29 £3,685k (further £915k reduction)
findings.quote: Revenue Support Grant 5,476 4,600 3,685 3,685 3,685

findings.paper_title: Appendix D Revenue Budget 2026-27, Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026 to 2031
findings.headline: Budget management reserve will need to be drawn to cover forecast gaps from 2027-28
findings.detail: The council's budget management reserve is forecast at £632k at 31 March 2026. The paper explicitly flags that reserves will be used: 'Members may require using some of this reserve to bridge future budget gaps 2027-28>'. With rising deficits outpacing identified savings, reserve depletion becomes material and limits future financial flexibility.
findings.matters: Reserves are finite. Repeated draws to cover budget shortfalls reduce cash buffers for service continuity or unexpected pressures, weakening financial resilience.
findings.figures: Budget management reserve forecast balance £632k at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: Members may require using some of this reserve to bridge future budget gaps 2027-28>

findings.paper_title: Appendix D Revenue Budget 2026-27, Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026 to 2031
findings.headline: Structural budget deficit emerges from 2027-28, growing to £2.882m by 2030-31 with no identified solution
findings.detail: The council's budget moves from balanced in 2026-27 to a £1.756m deficit in 2027-28, growing to £2.373m (2028-29), £2.6m (2029-30), and £2.882m (2030-31). The paper identifies no funding solutions to close these gaps. Government funding cuts (Revenue Support Grant from £5.476m to £3.685m) drive much of this structural pressure.
findings.matters: Growing structural deficits signal declining financial sustainability and force choices about service cuts, borrowing, or reserves depletion. Lenders need to understand how a council will close gaps this large.
findings.quote: Budget Gap / (Surplus) 0 1,756 2,373 2,600 2,882

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27, Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026 to 2031
findings.headline: Last-minute government funding change in February 2026 that created £1.1m in cumulative headwinds for 2027-28 and 2028-29
findings.detail: The Final Local Government Finance Settlement (9 Feb 2026) changed allocations due to a technical change in business rates pooling assumptions. This resulted in an additional £0.5m reduction for 2027-28 and a further £0.7m reduction for 2028-29 beyond the draft settlement, though the government awarded a one-off £0.5m Adjustment Support Grant for 2026-27 to smooth the immediate impact.
findings.matters: Late-stage funding changes create budgeting uncertainty and illustrate the council's vulnerability to technical changes in the funding formula; the council had to escalate concerns directly to the Minister to avoid the immediate hit.
findings.figures: One-off Adjustment Support Grant for 2026-27: £0.5m. Further reductions from draft to final: 2027-28 -£0.4m, 2028-29 -£0.7m
findings.quote: Prior to the above Final settlement being announced on 9 February 2026, we had been informed that this likely change was being implemented and had significant concerns that we could see an immediate reduction of £0.5million to the draft funding allocations for 2026-27, which would have had a significant detrimental effect upon our Council's financial position at such a last minute stage in the budget approval process.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27, Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026 to 2031
findings.headline: Capital programme dependent on unrealised receipts with downside risk from economic conditions
findings.detail: The £27.8m capital programme (2025-26 to 2027-28) is funded from capital receipts (£0.150m), borrowing (£13.3m), grants (£12.2m) and reserves (£2.1m). The council explicitly flags that receipts are "as yet unrealised" and that their value could decline due to economic conditions, forcing the council to seek additional external borrowing if receipts shortfall occurs.
findings.matters: If capital receipts fall short due to market conditions, the council will have to increase borrowing, adding interest costs to an already strained revenue budget.
findings.figures: Capital Programme 2025-26 to 2027-28: £27.772m. Planned funding: borrowing £13.294m, capital receipts £0.150m, grants/contributions £12.238m, reserves £2.090m
findings.quote: The Council faces two main risks in this area. The first is the fact that the Capital Programme is forecast to be funded from as yet unrealised receipts. The second is the ongoing value of receipts generated could be lower due to the economic situation. Both these factors could lead the Council to seek other sources of funding, such as increasing external borrowing

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27, Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026 to 2031
findings.headline: Business rates reset eliminates historic growth that has advantaged this council
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review 2.0 resets the business rates system for the first time since 2013-14, rebasing all historic growth to date and reallocating based on needs assessment. The council explicitly states it "has been significantly advantaged by these schemes" historically, but the reset means no further growth income is included in 2026-27 budget, with potential growth in 2027-28 not yet factored in.
findings.matters: The elimination of a historic revenue advantage that the council had relied on is a permanent structural change to the funding model; combined with the funding reduction, it significantly worsens the council's financial position.
findings.figures: Business Rates Renewable Energy Income in 2026-27 budget: £0.750m. No additional business rates growth factored into forward projections.
findings.quote: As members will be aware North Devon has been significantly advantaged by these schemes, the Fair Funding Review 2.0 is retaining the incentive of business growth, but it is rebasing all growth income to date and reallocating based on its needs assessment and then business rate retention to start again.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27, Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026 to 2031
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation to unitary status (April 2028) funded entirely by the council with no government grant
findings.detail: A new unitary authority is being formed in April 2028 as part of devolution, but the government has confirmed there is no additional funding to cover transition costs. The council is contributing £0.175m to a new LGR reserve for two years (to March 2028) to prepare for initial transition costs, with no visibility on total cost or post-2028 financial impact.
findings.matters: An unfunded, mandated organisational transformation creates uncertain financial liabilities and institutional uncertainty at a time when the council is already facing structural deficits.
findings.figures: LGR reserve contribution 2026-27 and 2027-28: £0.175m per year (£0.350m total)
findings.quote: The government have confirmed that there is no additional funding to cover transition costs to implement LGR and therefore the draft budget for 2026-27 includes a contribution of £0.175m to a new earmarked LGR reserve to start preparing for those initial transition costs that this Council will need to finance.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27, Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026 to 2031
findings.headline: Homelessness prevention costs continuing to increase with no ceiling identified
findings.detail: The council notes that demand for homelessness services has "continued to increase during 2025-26" and that "spend on this area has increased significantly in value since 2020." While a temporary accommodation reserve was created with £0.124m, the council has not needed to use it yet but expects demand to "continue through 2026-27." No upper limit or control mechanism is described.
findings.matters: Homelessness costs are demand-driven and largely outside the council's control; uncontrolled growth here will consume budget flexibility and potentially force cuts to discretionary services.
findings.figures: Temporary accommodation earmarked reserve: £0.124m created at 2023-24, forecast balance at 31 March 2027: £0.124m (unused)
findings.quote: Homelessness prevention measures in particular have increased over the past few years and as such demand for services such as temporary accommodation, where spend on this area has increased significantly in value since 2020. It is considered that in light of the current economic climate and general public sector finances that this will continue through 2026-27

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27, Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026 to 2031
findings.headline: Green Lanes Shopping Centre experiencing declining rental income despite cumulative profit to date
findings.detail: The £16m acquisition in 2021 has delivered a cumulative net return of £972,600 through 2024-25, but Quarter 3 2025-26 forecast shows a net rental income reduction of £206,000. The council notes this aligns with original projections from 2021 but acknowledges the retail market remains challenging, with Claire's Accessories and River Island going into administration. The council is working to let vacant units.
findings.matters: This is the council's primary commercial asset and a significant revenue generator; declining rental income suggests the commercial rationale for the acquisition is weakening, and the retail environment may deteriorate further.
findings.figures: Cumulative net return 2021-22 to 2024-25: £972,600. Forecast rental income reduction 2025-26: £206,000. Net rental projections 2026-27: £977k-£1,027k (down from £1,150k-£1,433k in prior years)
findings.quote: The retail market continues to be challenging and we have recently seen both Claire's Accessories and River Island going into administration – our team are working hard with our Asset Management partners to promote letting of these units and mitigate the financial impact upon us as the landlord through being a vacant unit.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27, Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026 to 2031
findings.headline: Growing medium-term budget gap of £2.9m by 2030-31, with no current plan to bridge it
findings.detail: Medium Term Financial Strategy shows cumulative budget gaps rising from zero in 2026-27 to £1.756m (2027-28), £2.373m (2028-29), £2.600m (2029-30) and £2.882m (2030-31). The council acknowledges this "creates a large budget gap to bridge moving forwards" and is relying on becoming "more entrepreneurial" and "commercially minded" to generate additional income, but no specific plans are detailed to meet these gaps.
findings.matters: A growing, unresolved structural deficit indicates the council may need to draw on reserves, cut services, or increase borrowing in future years, affecting its financial sustainability.
findings.quote: Clearly, this creates a large budget gap to bridge moving forwards, however it is crucial that both Officers and Members understand the potential financial context that we 'could' end up with.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Budget 2026-27, Capital Programme and Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026 to 2031
findings.headline: Real-terms funding reduction of 10% over three years, while rest of local government sector receives growth
findings.detail: Core Spending Power reduces from £19.1m (2026-27) to £17.9m (2028-29). Nominal reduction is 4.6%, but accounting for inflation running at 3% annually, the real-terms cut is 10%. The council describes shire district councils as being "side-lined" while the sector overall receives 5.7% increase in 2026-27. Council and local MP made direct representations to the Minister about the funding cuts.
findings.matters: This structural funding decline is the core driver of the council's budget pressures and will constrain its ability to maintain services and debt servicing over the medium term.
findings.figures: Core Spending Power 2026-27: £19.1m; 2027-28: £18.6m; 2028-29: £17.9m. Nominal reduction -4.6%, real-terms reduction -10%
findings.quote: Members need to be mindful though, that the real terms funding reduction is far greater than the above -4.6%; as the funding settlement does not take into account inflation, which has been running at around 3% annually recently. When you factor inflation into the above period the real-terms funding reduction between 2026-27 to 2028-29 is actually a reduction of -10%.

findings.paper_title: Bishop Fleming - Auditor's Annual Report
findings.headline: Carbon reduction commitment budgets remain unspecified after multi-year audit recommendation
findings.detail: An amber recommendation from prior years remains outstanding: the council does not explicitly identify budgets for meeting carbon reduction targets within its financial plans. Although a Carbon, Environment, and Biodiversity Plan was updated in September 2025 with some costings, the auditor notes this arrangement 'could be further enhanced if more of the options had costings included'.
findings.matters: An unresolved multi-year audit recommendation on budgeting for a stated policy commitment (carbon neutral by 2030) suggests the council may not be fully costing this significant obligation, potentially masking unfunded future costs.
findings.figures: Recommendation outstanding since at least 2023/24; partial costings only in September 2025 plan update
findings.quote: The Council does not explicitly identify budgets associated with meeting its carbon reduction targets, within its financial plans.

findings.paper_title: Bishop Fleming - Auditor's Annual Report
findings.headline: Budget Management Reserve drawn down to balance 2025/26 budget
findings.detail: The council faced a forecast budget gap of £0.487m for 2025/26 but achieved a balanced budget by withdrawing £0.164m from its Budget Management Reserve. This represents a shift from the council's recent record of achieving budget surpluses.
findings.matters: Drawing on reserves in the first year of forecast deficits signals reduced financial flexibility and raises questions about the council's ability to absorb the larger £3m+ annual gaps forecast for subsequent years.
findings.figures: £0.164m reserve withdrawal; £0.487m gap managed
findings.quote: This has required use of £0.164m of the Budget Management Reserve.

findings.paper_title: Bishop Fleming - Auditor's Annual Report
findings.headline: Council set to be dissolved as part of Local Government Reorganisation in the medium term
findings.detail: LGR was announced in December 2024, with the council facing dissolution and transfer of functions to a successor body. Discussions are ongoing between Devon councils on the preferred structure, with final proposals to government due November 2025. The Chief Executive noted the importance of engaging with this process despite the uncertainty.
findings.matters: The planned dissolution of the council in the medium term creates fundamental uncertainty about financial management continuity, long-term service delivery, and the viability of commitments made before the successor body is established.
findings.figures: Announcement December 2024; proposals due November 2025; dissolution in 'medium term'
findings.quote: The most significant challenge to the Council, like all other two-tier authorities, is the announcement of Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) in December 2024. LGR will mean that the Council will be dissolved in the medium term with its functions transferring to a successor body.

findings.paper_title: Bishop Fleming - Auditor's Annual Report
findings.headline: Budget gaps forecast to exceed £3m annually from 2026/27 onwards
findings.detail: The Medium Term Financial Strategy projects a budget gap of £0.487m in 2025/26, rising sharply to just under £3m per year from 2026/27 and over £3m per year from 2027/28 to 2029/30. The council has a strategy including service efficiencies and a Commercialisation Strategy to address these, but the scale of forecast deficits is material.
findings.matters: A council forecasting multi-million pound annual budget deficits over multiple years faces significant financial sustainability challenges and will require delivery of substantial savings or income growth to remain stable.
findings.figures: £0.487m (2025/26); just under £3m per year (2026/27); over £3m per year (2027/28 to 2029/30)
findings.quote: The MTFS for 2024/25 projected a breakeven position for the year, with budget gaps emerging over the life of the MTFS of £0.487m in 2025/26, rising sharply to just under £3m per year from 2026/27 to over £3m per year from 2027/28 to 2029/30.

findings.paper_title: Bishop Fleming - Audit Completion Report
findings.headline: Audit remains incomplete on material asset valuations, though clean opinion still anticipated
findings.detail: Work on valuation of land and buildings and pension fund net liability—both identified as significant audit risks—remains outstanding. The pension fund auditor's assurance letter was only recently received. Despite these incomplete procedures, the auditor states the anticipated opinion is unmodified, subject to satisfactory finalisation of these points.
findings.matters: Asset valuations (especially fixed assets and pension liabilities) are typically material to local authority balance sheets; delays in completing this core audit work is unusual and the dependency on pension fund auditor results could affect the final conclusion.
findings.figures: Pension fund auditor assurance letter only recently received; land and buildings valuations still under review
findings.quote: Our audit work has been satisfactorily completed on each of the above areas, with the exception of the valuation of the pension fund net liability where we have recently received the pension fund auditor's assurance letter and are currently in the process of completing procedures in this area, and the valuation of land and buildings... Our work in this area is ongoing.

findings.paper_title: Bishop Fleming - Audit Completion Report
findings.headline: First-year implementation of IFRS 16 leases is still undergoing audit testing
findings.detail: 2024/25 was the first year local government bodies were required to implement IFRS 16, bringing lease obligations onto the balance sheet as right-of-use assets and liabilities. Audit procedures on lease classification, valuation, and disclosure remain in progress as part of completion work.
findings.matters: IFRS 16 implementation materially changes balance sheet composition and financial ratios; lenders would want to ensure leases are correctly identified and valued, particularly for councils with significant lease obligations.
findings.figures: First year of implementation; leases testing among outstanding completion procedures
findings.quote: 2024/25 was the first year in which local government bodies were required to implement the provisions of IFRS 16 leases... Leases testing (including IFRS 16)... Our work on this area is ongoing.

findings.paper_title: Bishop Fleming - Audit Completion Report
findings.headline: Segregation of duties weakness in Civica system remains unresolved after multiple audit cycles
findings.detail: Finance team members retain both financial and administrative privileges on the Civica accounting system, a combination that creates risk of bypassing system-enforced controls. This issue was flagged in 2023/24 with a recommendation for remediation; the 2024/25 audit found it still unresolved. The auditor's recommendation remains unchanged. Management maintains these combined privileges are operationally necessary because finance staff, not ICT, understand the system well enough to configure access correctly.
findings.matters: Unresolved control weaknesses that persist across audit cycles indicate weak governance response; segregation of duties is fundamental to fraud prevention and would be a concern for any lender assessing control environment.
findings.figures: Issue outstanding since at least 2023/24
findings.quote: We have reviewed the access rights held by users on Civica and identified that members of the Finance Team retain both financial and administrative privileges... 2024/25 Recommendation: Our recommendation remains unchanged.

news_drafts.lead: The service requires recurring general fund support to cover the income gap, which impacts the councils' financial sustainability. The substantial favorable variance signals strong financial management and realistic cost discipline in a partnership…

news_drafts.lead: Rising borrowing rates will increase debt service costs on the council's £36.3m capital financing requirement and any future capital borrowing
